1.title: Remotes: Clone, Fetch, Pull, Push
1.text: Welcome to Module seven: Remotes: Clone, Fetch, Pull, Push. It covers the exam area Part three: Working with remotes. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do seven things. Add a remote and clone a repository. Push with upstream tracking. Tell fetch from pull. Read ahead and behind. Fix a rejected push. Use force-with-lease safely. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Course
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the course. Part: Part three: Working with remotes. Verified with: Git two point five zero.one: every command was run in the lab.

1.title: A remote is another repository
1.text: A remote is another repository. A remote is another Git repository that yours can send commits to and receive commits from. On Git Hub it is a repository on a server. In the lab it is a bare repository, made with git init the bare flag: it holds the history and no working files, which is what a shared repository needs. By convention the main remote is called origin.

1.title: A remote is another repository, continued
1.text: A remote is another repository. The figure shows this: Two developers each have a local repository and exchange commits through one shared remote repository with push, fetch and pull.

1.title: A remote is another repository, continued
1.text: A remote is another repository. git remote add name url. Connects your repository to a remote under a name. git remote dash v. Lists remotes with their fetch and push U R Ls. git clone url folder. Copies a remote: history, a remote named origin, a checkout of the default branch. git push dash u origin main. Sends main and sets its upstream. git ls remote origin. Lists the branches and head on the remote without fetching.

1.title: A remote is another repository, continued
1.text: A remote is another repository. The upstream of a branch is the remote branch it follows. It is stored as branch dot main dot remote and branch dot main dot merge, and it lets a plain git push and git pull work without arguments. A clone sets it for you. Try it. Connect Ada's repository to the shared remote. Your hashes will differ.

1.title: Fetch, pull and remote-tracking branches
1.text: Fetch, pull and remote-tracking branches. origin slash main is a remote-tracking branch: your own record of where main was on origin the last time you talked to it. You cannot commit on it. Only fetch, pull and push move it. git fetch. Downloads new commits and moves origin slash; changes no branch and no file of yours. git pull. git fetch plus a merge (or a ree base) into your current branch. git pull the ff only flag. Pulls only if a fast-forward is possible; otherwise it stops.

1.title: Fetch, pull and remote-tracking branches, continued
1.text: Fetch, pull and remote-tracking branches. Ahead and behind are easy to read. git branch dash v v shows origin slash main behind one or ahead one, and git status -sb shows the same on its first line. Two ranges give the commits. git log main dot dot origin slash main lists what you would get. git log origin slash main dot dot main lists what you would send. Try it. Bob looks before he changes anything.

1.text: Fetch, pull and remote-tracking branches. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.text: Fetch, pull and remote-tracking branches. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Tip: Fetch whenever you like: it never changes your work. Fetch first, read the log, then decide how to integrate.

1.title: A rejected push, and the fix
1.text: A rejected push, and the fix. A push is accepted only if it fast-forwards the remote branch. If a teammate pushed first, the remote holds commits you lack, and Git rejects your push. The message ends with fetch first when you have not fetched yet, and with non fast forward after a fetch. Try it. Reproduce it with Ada and Bob. Ada's push fails, and she fixes it.

1.title: A rejected push, and the fix, continued
1.text: A rejected push, and the fix. After that, a plain git push works. There are two honest fixes, and force is not one of them. git pull the ree base flag. What it does: Replays your commits on top of the fetched ones. History: Linear. git fetch, then git merge origin slash main. What it does: Joins the two lines with a merge commit. History: Keeps both lines.

1.title: A rejected push, and the fix, continued
1.text: A rejected push, and the fix. Plain git pull on diverged branches makes this Git stop with "Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches", and git pull the ff only flag stops with "Not possible to fast-forward". Choose once with git config pull dot ree base true to ree base on every pull, or git config pull dot ff only to refuse anything but a fast-forward. Add the global flag to set a choice for every repository. Tip: A rejected push means someone pushed first: fetch and integrate, never force. Forcing throws their commits away.

1.title: Force pushes, new branches and clean-up
1.text: Force pushes, new branches and clean-up. A force push moves the remote branch to your version even when that discards commits. git push the force flag. Overwrites the remote branch no matter what. git push the force with lease flag. Refuses when the remote branch moved since your last fetch.

1.title: Force pushes, new branches and clean-up, continued
1.text: Force pushes, new branches and clean-up. In the lab Bob pushed, and Ada, who had not fetched, amended her commit. the force with lease flag refused with stale info, but plain the force flag went through and Bob's commit vanished from the remote. It stayed in Bob's clone. The lease only guards what you have not fetched: after a fetch the same push passes, so look at what you are about to overwrite.

1.title: Force pushes, new branches and clean-up, continued
1.text: Force pushes, new branches and clean-up. New branches. A new branch has no upstream, so git push fails with "has no upstream branch". Use git push dash u origin branch once, or git config push dot auto Setup Remote true. In the other direction, git switch name creates a local branch that tracks origin slash name when only the remote one exists. Deleting. git push origin the delete flag branch removes the branch on the remote, and your local branch stays. Teammates keep a stale origin slash branch until they run git fetch the prune flag. The setting fetch dot prune true does that on every fetch.

2.text: Force pushes, new branches and clean-up. Try it. Refuse a stale force, delete a remote branch, then prune. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

2.text: Force pushes, new branches and clean-up. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Tip: Use git push the force with lease flag, never plain the force flag. It refuses when someone else pushed first.

2.title: More than one remote
2.text: More than one remote. A repository can have several remotes. The common second name is upstream: the original repository when you work from your own copy (module eight). Each remote has its own remote-tracking branches, such as upstream slash main. git remote add upstream url. Adds a second remote. git fetch upstream. Fetches from that remote only. git push upstream main. Pushes to that remote by name. git remote set url origin url. Changes where a remote points, for example after a move. git remote get url origin. Prints the U R L a remote uses.

2.text: More than one remote. Try it. Add a second remote and look at the refs on it. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. After git fetch, git branch dash v v shows main six five six c eight three seven origin slash main behind one Add readme. What is true now? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Your main branch still points at the old commit. Fetch only moves origin slash main, so you are one commit behind until you merge or pull.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Bob's git push is rejected, and the message ends with fetch first. What should he do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Run git fetch, merge or ree base, then push again. The remote has commits he lacks, so he fetches, rebases or merges them in, and pushes again.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Ada runs git push the force with lease flag and Git prints stale info. What does that mean? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: The remote branch moved since her last fetch. The lease compares the remote with her last fetch, and a teammate's push made them differ.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. git log origin slash main dot dot main prints two commits. What does that tell you? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Two commits exist on your branch that origin lacks. The range lists commits reachable from main but not from origin slash main, which are the ones a push would send.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. The team wants a plain git pull to replay local commits on top of fetched ones and keep history linear. Which setting does that? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: git config pull dot ree base true, which rebases on every pull. With pull dot ree base true, a pull fetches and then rebases the local commits instead of merging.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Ada deleted feature slash wishlist with git push origin the delete flag feature slash wishlist. Bob's git branch dash r still lists origin slash feature slash wishlist. How does he remove it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: git fetch the prune flag, which drops stale tracking branches. A plain fetch keeps stale remote-tracking branches, and the prune flag removes the ones whose remote branch is gone.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Which command connects an existing repository to a remote named origin? Answer: git remote add origin url. Question two. What does the dash u in git push dash u origin main set up? Answer: The upstream, so a plain git push and git pull work later. Question three. What does git pull do? Answer: It runs git fetch and then merges, or rebases, into the current branch.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What does origin slash main record? Answer: Where main was on origin at your last fetch, push or pull. Question five. Which push option is safer than the force flag? Answer: the force with lease flag. Question six. Which command changes the U R L a remote points to? Answer: git remote set url name url.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Remote: another repository; the lab uses a bare one; origin is the usual name. Setup: git remote add, git remote dash v, git clone, git push dash u origin main. Tracking: the upstream is set by a clone or push dash u. Fetch and pull: fetch only moves origin slash; pull is fetch plus merge or ree base. Ahead and behind: git status -sb, git branch dash v v; main dot dot origin slash main to get, origin slash main dot dot main to send. Rejected push: someone pushed first: fetch, then pull the ree base flag or merge, then push. Force: the force with lease flag refuses after others pushed; plain the force flag overwrites. Clean-up: git push origin the delete flag branch; git fetch the prune flag; fetch dot prune true. Several remotes: git remote add upstream, git fetch upstream, set url, ls remote.
